q: According to NACFE's dedicated TCO report, what does it conclude about the total cost of ownership comparison across the four Messy Middle powertrains?
expect: BEVs are projected to achieve the lowest net TCO of any powertrain in every one of the five modeled duty cycles by 2035, driven by falling battery/vehicle prices, while diesel faces a 'cost escalator' (rising maintenance, insurance, and emissions-compliance costs) that erodes its current advantage even as fuel cost per mile drops slightly. Per-duty-cycle 2035 figures include: Long-Haul OTR, diesel's current $0.61/mile advantage flips, with BEVs undercutting diesel by $0.09/mile; Regional Linehaul, BEV $0.94/mile vs. diesel $1.00/mile; Regional RTB, BEV $1.13/mile vs. diesel $1.29/mile (a 12% BEV advantage); Urban/Metro P&D, BEV $1.92/mile vs. diesel $2.43/mile; Drayage/Port Shuttles, BEV about $0.19/mile cheaper than diesel. CNG/RNG serves as a stable near-term hedge but is eventually overtaken by BEVs in most duty cycles; FCEV remains the most expensive option through 2035, tethered to hydrogen delivery price ($4-$15/kg modeled). The analysis assumes no incentives, as a conservative baseline.
loc: TCO report, Section 1.4-1.5 (Key Findings by Powertrain / by Duty Cycle)

q: What has NACFE found about total cost of ownership for last-mile electric delivery vans?
expect: NACFE's 2024 Electric DEPOT report found last-mile electric vans/step vans already have upfront costs much closer to parity with gas/diesel than heavier Class 8 vehicles, and classifies them as 'small energy depots' (under 10 MWh/day) that are 'ready to electrify now' because long overnight dwell times allow slow, low-cost managed charging that avoids demand charges. Real examples tracked: Frito-Lay's Ford E-Transit vans (68-kWh battery, ~108-mile range) in Queens, NY, and Purolator's Motiv EPIC step vans (127-kWh battery, ~105-mile range, 4-60 mile daily routes) in Richmond, BC. NACFE cautions that standard TCO spreadsheets often miss uptime gains, the fleet's operational learning curve, and regional incentives like California's LCFS credits. Note this is a narrower/different scope than the 2026 TCO report, which models Class 8 vehicles only and does not cover vans.
loc: p.34 (Frito-Lay E-Transit), p.43 (Purolator Motiv EPIC), p.77-79 (small energy depot framing, Figure 57)

In the actual 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle, run in real revenue service (not a controlled demo), NACFE tracked a Windrose battery-electric sleeper (Joyride Logistics) with a real-world quoted range of up to 420 miles, and its Initial Findings list '400+ mile battery electric vehicles' among recent powertrain advancements — roughly double the typical 2023 production range, achieved in normal fleet duty cycles rather than a one-off demonstration.

q: NACFE's 2023 white paper laid out a suggested sequence for fleets choosing a powertrain (start with BEV, then hydrogen fuel cell, then natural gas/hybrids/renewable fuels, then efficient diesel as a fallback), while also acknowledging this was 'an oversimplification.' expect: The 2023 white paper's 'Framework for Powertrain Decision Making' (Figure 15) suggests fleets start with BEV, fall back to hydrogen fuel cell, then natural gas/hybrids/renewable fuels, and finally efficient diesel, while explicitly noting fleets will likely need multiple, duty-cycle-specific decisions rather than one universal answer. NACFE reused this same framework graphic in the 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle report, and that Run's real-world findings confirmed the 2023 premise rather than crowning one winner: 'the real-world results are that all four technologies are performing well in this segment of the market and there is no one right choice for all fleets. Rather powertrain choice depends on the intricacies of each fleet's operation, the length of haul, access to fueling/charging and a host of other factors.'
